AAAI 2024’s Adaptive Hardness Negative Sampling (AHNS) supports controlling negative difficulty, but does not directly validate a uniform warm-up followed by fixed moderate-rank selection. AHNS samples a small pool of uninteracted items, scores them with the current model, and selects the negative closest to a target score determined by the corresponding positive’s score. Its criteria require positive-specific, adjustable hardness that decreases as positive confidence increases. Experiments show harder negatives early and easier negatives later; the paper explicitly identifies limitations of epoch-only curricula. [Paper](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/download/28709/29371)

Evidence comes from matrix factorization with BPR on MovieLens and three Amazon datasets, rather than sequential BERT4Rec. Comparisons include uniform negatives, hardest-candidate sampling, controllable-rank DNS, and curriculum sampling. AHNS outperforms these baselines; hardness trajectories and hyperparameter studies support its rationale, but do not isolate warm-up or moderate-rank selection. False-negative mitigation is inferred from training behavior and ranking performance, rather than verified negative labels. Candidate pools range from 4–64; runtime is comparable to basic hard-negative mining, while uniform sampling remains cheapest. [Experiments](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.05191v1#S4)

For the proposed BERT4Rec experiment, this provides methodological motivation for model-scored negatives while avoiding persistent hardest-only mining. A fixed warm-up/moderate-rank curriculum remains a hypothesis requiring validation against uniform sampling under matched compute. Prioritize that sampling ablation before adding temporal or text architecture changes; AHNS does not establish transfer to masked-target training or the pinned HR@10 evaluation.
